steps.body: Both fractions must be renamed. In the model, 1/2 scales by 3 and 1/3 scales by 2 so both fractions arrive at sixths.
steps.narration: Both fractions must be renamed. In the model, 1/2 scales by 3 and 1/3 scales by 2 so both fractions arrive at sixths.

widget.successFeedback: 2/12 — sixths scale by 2 to reach twelfths, while fourths scale by 3.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 2/12 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 2/12 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: 3/12 is what 1/4 becomes; a sixth is smaller and scales to 2/12.
1/12 is a single twelfth; a sixth holds two of them.

predict.prompt: Renaming 1/4 and 1/6 into twelfths, same scaling factor?
predict.reveal: Each denominator needs whatever factor carries IT to twelve, and 4 and 6 need different ones.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u rename.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u rename a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Scale 1/6 by ×2 on top and bottom. What is the new numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: Scaling by ×2 has to reach the top as well, or the fraction's value changes.
That scaled the DENOMINATOR; the question asks what sits on top afterwards.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.

concept.body: A common denominator lets 1/2 and 1/3 share the same piece size: sixths. Renaming never changes either fraction's value — each fraction is scaled up by whatever factor turns its OWN denominator into 6, and that factor can differ from one fraction to the next.
concept.narration: A common denominator lets 1/2 and 1/3 share the same piece size: sixths. Renaming never changes either fraction's value — each fraction is scaled up by whatever factor turns its OWN denominator into 6, and that factor can differ from one fraction to the next.

widget.prompt: To rename 1/4 and 1/6 both to twelfths, a learner scales both by ×3. What is wrong with that plan?

options.label: 1/6 needs ×2, not ×3 — only 1/4 needs ×3 to reach twelfths
options.feedback: Correct — 1/4 scales by 3 to reach 3/12, but 1/6 only needs ×2 to reach 2/12; each fraction gets its own factor.

options.label: Nothing is wrong; ×3 works for both
options.feedback: Scaling 1/6 by ×3 gives 3/18, not twelfths at all — the factor must match each fraction's own denominator gap.

options.label: Both fractions need ×6 instead
options.feedback: ×6 way overshoots; 1/4 needs only ×3 and 1/6 needs only ×2 to land on twelfths.

options.label: The numerators should be added instead
options.feedback: Renaming scales top and bottom together; it never adds the numerators of the two original fractions.
